title: Relational & Equality Operators
summary: Compare values with >, <, >=, <=, ==, and != to produce boolean results for conditional decision-making.
learningObjectives: Test equality using == and inequality using !=
Understand that comparison expressions always evaluate to a boolean (true or false)
Avoid common bugs like using = instead of == or comparing Strings with ==
expectedOutcomes: Write accurate conditional comparisons for real-world thresholds like age and passing marks
Confidently distinguish between primitive equality and reference equality

activities.title: Comparing Values in Java
activities.content:
### What are Relational and Equality Operators?

Every decision in software begins with a comparison:
- Has the student scored at least 40 marks to pass? (`marks >= 40`)
- Is the user's age 18 or older to vote? (`age >= 18`)
- Is the item out of stock? (`quantity == 0`)

Comparison operators take two operands and **always return a `boolean` result: `true` or `false`**.

---

### 1. Relational Operators

Relational operators compare the relative magnitude of numeric values:

| Operator | Meaning | Example | When is it true? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `>` | Greater than | `age > 18` | `age` is 19 or above |
| `<` | Less than | `speed < 60` | `speed` is 59 or below |
| `>=` | Greater than or equal to | `marks >= 40` | `marks` is 40 or above |
| `<=` | Less than or equal to | `cart <= 1000` | `cart` is 1000 or below |

```java
int marks = 75;
boolean isPassed = marks >= 40; // true
boolean isDistinction = marks >= 75; // true
```

---

### 2. Equality Operators (`==` and `!=`)

| Operator | Meaning | Example | When is it true? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `==` | Equal to | `a == b` | If `a` and `b` hold identical values |
| `!=` | Not equal to | `a != b` | If `a` and `b` hold different values |

```java
int rollA = 101;
int rollB = 102;

System.out.println(rollA == rollB); // false
System.out.println(rollA != rollB); // true
```

---

### 3. Critical Mistakes to Avoid

> [!CAUTION]
> **Trap 1: `=` vs `==`**:
> `=` assigns a value. `==` checks for equality.
> Writing `if (marks = 50)` is a compiler error in Java because `50` is an integer, not a boolean condition.

> [!WARNING]
> **Trap 2: Comparing Strings with `==`**:
> For primitive types (`int`, `double`, `char`), `==` compares the raw values.
> But for reference types like `String`, `==` compares **memory addresses**, NOT text content!
> Always compare Strings using `.equals()`:
> ```java
> String s1 = new String("Java");
> String s2 = new String("Java");
> System.out.println(s1 == s2);      // false (different heap memory addresses!)
> System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // true (compares text content)
> ```

> [!NOTE]
> **Trap 3: Floating-Point Equality**:
> Because of IEEE 754 precision quirks, `(0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3` is `false`! Never test floats for strict equality with `==`.

---

### Code Walkthrough

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int studentAge = 19;
        int passMarksCutoff = 40;
        int studentMarks = 82;
        
        boolean canVote = studentAge >= 18;
        boolean hasPassed = studentMarks >= passMarksCutoff;
        boolean hasPerfectScore = studentMarks == 100;
        boolean hasIncompleteScore = studentMarks != 0;
        
        System.out.println("Eligible to Vote: " + canVote);
        System.out.println("Passed Exam: " + hasPassed);
        System.out.println("Perfect 100: " + hasPerfectScore);
        System.out.println("Exam Attempted: " + hasIncompleteScore);
    }
}
```

breakdown.whatIsIt: Relational (>, <, >=, <=) and equality (==, !=) operators compare two values and produce a boolean (true or false).
breakdown.whyItMatters: All program branching, if-else logic, and input validation depend on comparison results.
howItWorks: Relational operators compare magnitudes of numbers.
Equality operators (==, !=) test for identical values.
The result is strictly a boolean value (true or false).
keyTakeaways: Comparison operators always evaluate to true or false.
Never confuse assignment (=) with equality comparison (==).
Use .equals() for String text comparison, not ==.
Avoid checking exact equality on float/double due to binary rounding.

questions.prompt: What data type is returned by comparison operators like '>' and '==' in Java?
questions.question: What data type is returned by comparison operators like '>' and '==' in Java?
questions.explanation: All relational and equality operators strictly evaluate to a boolean: true or false.
hints: Java does not use 1/0 for truth values.

questions.question: What will System.out.println(15 >= 15); output?
questions.explanation: The >= operator checks if the left value is greater than OR equal to the right value. Since 15 equals 15, it evaluates to true.
hints: It checks greater than OR equal to.

questions.prompt: Which operator checks if two values are NOT equal in Java?
questions.question: Which operator checks if two values are NOT equal in Java?
questions.explanation: In Java, != is the not-equal-to equality operator.

questions.prompt: What will System.out.println('A' == 65); output in Java?
questions.question: What will System.out.println('A' == 65); output in Java?
questions.explanation: In Java, char is a numeric 16-bit Unicode type. 'A' has the Unicode/ASCII code 65, so 'A' == 65 compares 65 == 65, which is true.
hints: Characters have underlying numeric Unicode values.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid using == to compare two String objects in Java?
questions.question: Why should you avoid using == to compare two String objects in Java?
options: == only compares memory addresses (object references), not character contents
== is not allowed on Strings and causes a compiler error
Strings must be converted to int before comparing
questions.explanation: On reference types, == checks if both references point to the exact same heap memory address. To compare text characters, you must use .equals().
hints: Consider reference equality vs value equality.

questions.prompt: What is the output of System.out.println((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3); in Java?
questions.question: What is the output of System.out.println((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3); in Java?
questions.explanation: Due to binary IEEE 754 floating-point representation, 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004, which does not equal 0.3. Hence false is printed.
hints: Remember the floating-point precision imprecision discussed in Module 2.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: Relational & Equality Operators

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between '==' and '.equals()' when comparing objects in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `==` is an operator that compares memory addresses (reference equality) to check if two variables point to the exact same object in the heap. In contrast, `.equals()` is a method designed to compare the actual semantic content or state of the objects (content equality). For primitives, always use `==`; for Strings and objects, use `.equals()`.
keyPoints: == compares heap memory references; .equals() compares actual data values.

interviewQA.question: Can you compare a char with an int using relational operators in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. In Java, `char` is an integral type backed by 16-bit unsigned Unicode values. When comparing a `char` and an `int` (e.g. `'A' < 100`), Java automatically widens the `char` to its numeric code point (`65 < 100`), which evaluates to `true`.
keyPoints: Chars promote automatically to their numeric Unicode code points during comparisons.

interviewQA.question: Why is testing float or double variables with '==' considered bad practice in production?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Binary floating-point numbers (IEEE 754) cannot represent most decimal fractions (like 0.1) exactly. Calculations accumulate tiny rounding errors (e.g. `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`). In production, you should test if `Math.abs(a - b) < EPSILON` where EPSILON is a small threshold like `0.00001`, or use `BigDecimal`.
keyPoints: Never compare floats with ==; check if the absolute difference is within a small epsilon.

interviewQA.question: What is the result of 'true == false' and can boolean values be compared with '>' or '<'?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `true == false` evaluates to `false`. However, boolean variables CANNOT be compared using relational operators like `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`. Writing `true > false` causes a compile-time error because booleans have no numeric magnitude or ordering in Java.
keyPoints: Booleans can be checked with == and !=, but relational operators (>, <) are illegal.

interviewQA.question: What happens if a developer mistakenly writes 'if (isApproved = true)' in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Single `=` is assignment. `isApproved = true` assigns `true` to `isApproved` and evaluates to the assigned boolean value (`true`). Thus, the `if` condition always passes! To prevent this, developers should simply write `if (isApproved)` or use `==`.
keyPoints: if (b = true) assigns true and always executes; write if (b) instead.
